title: CPU Scheduling
html:
CPU allocation algorithms, Gantt chart scheduling evaluations, and queue strategies.

1. Scheduling Terms & Definitions

• Preemption: The OS can interrupt a running process to allocate CPU to another process.
• Non-preemption: A process holds the CPU until it terminates or blocks (voluntarily relinquishes control).
• Arrival Time (AT): Time when a process enters the ready queue.
• Burst Time (BT): CPU execution time required by the process.
• Completion Time (CT): Time when the process finishes execution.
• Turnaround Time (TAT): Total time from arrival to completion. TAT = CT - AT.
• Waiting Time (WT): Time spent waiting in the ready queue. WT = TAT - BT.
• Response Time (RT): Time from arrival to the first CPU allocation. RT = First Allocation - AT.

First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)

Definition: Non-preemptive scheduling where the process that requests the CPU first is allocated the CPU first, managed via a standard FIFO queue.
Pros
  • Simple to understand, code, and maintain.
  • Fairness in terms of order of requests; guarantees no starvation.
Cons
  • Convoy Effect: Short processes get stuck waiting behind long CPU-bound processes.
  • Poor average waiting and response times; unsuitable for interactive systems.

Use Case: Batch systems where turnaround time is secondary to CPU utilization, or simple microcontroller task queues.

Shortest Job First (SJF)

Definition: Non-preemptive scheduling that selects the waiting process with the smallest CPU burst time for the next execution slot.
Pros
  • Provably minimizes average waiting time for a given set of processes.
  • Good for short interactive processes which finish quickly.
Cons
  • Starvation: Long processes can wait indefinitely if short processes are constantly submitted.
  • Impossible to know next CPU burst length beforehand (must be predicted).

Use Case: Long-term scheduler in mainframe environments where execution time limits are declared in job attributes.

Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)

Definition: Preemptive version of SJF. The currently running process is preempted if a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining burst time.
Pros
  • Achieves exceptionally low average waiting time and response time.
  • Overcomes the non-preemptive delays of SJF when short jobs arrive.
Cons
  • High context-switch overhead due to frequent preemption checks.
  • Requires tracking remaining burst times continuously; starvation risk.

Use Case: Short-term CPU schedulers in environments where process runtimes are predictable or bounded.

Round Robin (RR) — Time Quantum = 2

Definition: Preemptive scheduling algorithm where each ready process is assigned the CPU for a fixed time interval (time quantum) in a cyclic order.
Pros
  • Highly interactive; guarantees excellent response times for all users.
  • Fair distribution of CPU resources; completely starvation-free.
Cons
  • Heavy performance degradation if the quantum is too small (excessive context switching).
  • Becomes FCFS if the time quantum is larger than the longest burst time.

Use Case: Multi-user time-sharing environments, general desktop systems, and network packet routing.

Preemptive Priority Scheduling

Definition: CPU scheduling where tasks are assigned priorities, and a higher priority process preempts a lower priority running process.
Pros
  • Critical and time-sensitive processes are prioritized and execute immediately.
  • Allows direct control over system responsiveness for important tasks.
Cons
  • Indefinite Blocking / Starvation: Low priority processes may never run if high priority tasks stream in.
  • Requires complex priority assignment; solved by aging (gradually increasing priority over wait time).

Use Case: Real-time operating systems (RTOS) or critical daemon process scheduling inside modern operating kernels.

Scheduling Mechanics

How to choose Round Robin Quantum?

Choosing the time quantum clock size is a critical trade-off:

  • Too small: Excessive context switching overhead destroys efficiency.
  • Too large: Becomes identical to First-Come First-Served (FCFS), resulting in terrible response times for interactive applications.
  • Rule of Thumb: 80% of CPU bursts should be shorter than the time quantum.

Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)

One of the most complex scheduler types. It organizes the ready queue into multiple priority tiers. Processes can migrate dynamically: CPU-bound processes drop to lower priority queues, while I/O-bound processes migrate upwards. This maximizes interactive responsiveness without requiring process profiling.
